title: Learning to Correct: Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Attempt Chain-of-Thought
claim: Standard and naive credit-assignment schemes are high-variance or biased; our calibrated per-step weighting gives unbiased, low-variance learning and best performance.
layout: 3 stacked rows, top-to-bottom, green highlighted final row with warning badges
description: Three horizontal rounded panels are stacked vertically, each showing the same chain of three boxes labeled Attempt 1, Attempt 2 and Attempt 3, joined by small arrows. The top gray panel, TL (Trajectory-Level), has an orange 'high variance' warning badge and a dark banner saying the same reward r1=r2=r3 is assigned to all attempts. The middle gray panel, NAL (Naive Attempt-Level), has a blue 'weights = 1 (uniform)' tag, an orange 'biased' warning, and dark labels Reward: r1, r2 and r3 under each attempt. The bottom panel, CAL (Calibrated Attempt-Level), is tinted green with a smiley face, a green check badge reading 'best Ver@K', and green labels Weight: w1·r1, w2·r2 and w3·r3. The eye goes first to the green bottom panel and the warning badges.
caption: We consider RLOO and GRPO methods that weigh individual attempts. TL is the standard approach that uses the final Ver@K reward for all attempts. NAL uses per-attempt pass/fail as weights. Proposed CAL approach calibrates naive weights to obtain unbiased low-variance gradients.
abstract: State-of-the-art reasoning models utilize long chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve increasingly complex problems using more test-time computation. In this work, we explore a long CoT setting where the model makes up to K successive attempts at solving a problem, in which each attempt is allowed to build on earlier ones after the model receives a hard verifier feedback. This motivates RL methods that can harness per-attempt rewards by carefully weighting individual attempts. We study optimizing the Verification@K reward (the model succeeds by the K-th attempt) and show that naively weighing the attempts by their pass/fail results in biased gradients. We introduce Calibrated Attempt-Level (CAL) GRPO by devising a weighing strategy to obtain unbiased gradients while maintaining small variance. Our theory reveals how incorporating per-attempt rewards influence the training and the eventual Verification@K performance. Experiments, baselines, and ablations on synthetic and real data corroborate our theory and the benefits of CAL-GRPO over vanilla GRPO as well as naive weighting.
